case_study_insert.main_stem: Suncoast Travel Tours (STT) is a partnership in the travel and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Marcus Hale, it sells coastal coach holidays to regional travellers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. STT plans to invest $450,000 in a fleet of newer coaches, financed by hire purchase and $150,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $200 per tour package and a selling price of $320 per tour package, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. STT faces two problems: coach breakdowns have cancelled tours and complaints about late documentation have risen sharply, threatening repeat bookings.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Tour Operations Extract, Q3 2025: STT sold 7,200 package tours last quarter at an average price of $320, with 4.6% of tours cancelled because of coach breakdowns. Customer complaints rose from 19 to 34 per month and delivery of confirmation documents took 6 days against a 2-day target. A survey of 400 clients found 72% would choose an operator with newer coaches and 58% valued flexible booking. Driver retraining on the new coach systems costs $380 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Suncoast Travel Tours as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $12.40 to $13.23 per hour from April 2026. (3) Diesel and coach-maintenance input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while domestic holiday spending grew 3.8% and inflation is 6.4%.

questions.question_text: STT is acquiring its $450,000 coach fleet. Explain two advantages for STT of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $450,000 cost into regular instalments, so STT does not need the full sum upfront and can preserve cash for the $600,000 fixed costs and the 6 days currently needed to send documents. Because the loan is secured on the coaches themselves, the lender has less need for other collateral, protecting the partnership's other assets while the new fleet cuts the 4.6% cancellation rate.

Point 2: STT gains use of the newer coaches immediately and can start winning the 72% of surveyed clients who prefer an operator with newer vehicles, generating the $320 per tour needed to meet instalments. This is valuable while the base rate has risen to 5.5% and domestic holiday spending is up only 3.8%, since hire-purchase payments are fixed and easier to budget than a variable-rate bank loan, so the 72% of clients who prefer newer coaches can be won without taking on more debt.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to STT's fleet decision and finances.

questions.question_text: STT wants to promote its newer coach holidays. Consider bus-stop posters, partnerships with travel agents, or short video adverts on social media. Which should STT choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Bus-stop posters: Posters are cheap and can be placed in coastal towns near STT's routes, giving repeated local exposure. However, they cannot show the comfort of the new coaches, reach is limited to passers-by, and there is no way to measure bookings, which is a problem when 4.6% of tours are already cancelled and the $450,000 fleet must be filled.

Partnerships with travel agents: Agents already meet holidaymakers at the moment they book and can recommend STT's newer coaches to the 72% of 400 surveyed clients who prefer modern vehicles, while explaining the flexible booking valued by 58%. Commission is paid only on sales, so cost is linked to revenue, which suits a partnership with $600,000 fixed costs. The drawback is that agents take a share of the $320 price and may favour larger competitors.

Short video adverts on social media: Video can show the new coaches and flexible booking to a wide audience at modest cost and can be tracked. Yet results depend on algorithms and constant content, and viewers outside the coastal market may never buy a package, so spend can be wasted.

Recommendation: STT should choose travel-agent partnerships. They reach buyers at the point of purchase, convert the 72% preference for newer coaches into bookings, and keep costs tied to sales, unlike untargeted posters or unmeasurable video ads. Posters are rejected for narrow, unmeasurable reach and video advertising for uncertain conversion; agent commission is affordable against the $320 price and the 3.8% growth in domestic holidays, and agent feedback can guide service improvements.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to STT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in STT's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in STT's context with a justified recommendation explaining why posters and video adverts are rejected.

questions.question_text: STT's coach cancellations have reached 4.6% and complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for STT of its laissez-faire leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives STT's 40 experienced drivers freedom to choose the quickest routes and to arrange replacements when a coach breaks down, which can reduce the 4.6% cancellation rate without waiting for head-office approval. In a flat structure this speeds decisions and helps deliver the 7,200 package tours sold last quarter on time, protecting the $320 revenue per package.

Point 2: Trusting capable drivers to solve problems raises their motivation and ownership of service quality, which can cut the 34 monthly complaints about documents because drivers can chase paperwork locally. Autonomy also reduces the need for supervisors, saving on the $380-per-employee retraining budget and letting STT focus resources on the $450,000 coach fleet. In a 40-person partnership, autonomy also cuts supervision costs and lets drivers work to the 2-day document target locally; the flat structure keeps decisions close to the action. That protects the 58% of clients who value flexible booking and depend on timely confirmations.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to STT cancellations, complaints and structure.

questions.question_text: STT must prepare new drivers for the coach fleet. Consider formal induction training or on-the-job training. Which should STT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Formal induction training: A structured induction explains STT's booking system, safety procedures and the 2-day document target, which directly addresses the 6 days currently taken to send confirmations and the 34 monthly complaints; consistent paperwork would also appeal to the 72% of clients who want professionally run operators. It gives every driver the same standards and a record of competence. It takes drivers away from routes, however, costs $380 per employee, and generic content may not cover the practical handling of the newer coaches.

On-the-job training: Learning on real routes means drivers master the actual coaches and local roads immediately, keeping tours running while the 4.6% cancellation rate is tackled, and it costs nothing in course fees. It suits the laissez-faire culture and the 40-strong workforce. Its weakness is that bad habits can spread, standards vary, and documentation errors may persist because no formal system is taught, while 4.6% cancellations mean every route day counts and keeping drivers working as they learn has real value.

Decision: STT should choose formal induction followed by on-the-job coaching. The induction fixes the document delays and sets consistent safety standards, which protects the $450,000 fleet investment, while route coaching keeps the training practical. Pure on-the-job training is rejected because it would leave the 6-day documentation problem and the 34 complaints unsolved, even though it is cheaper and less disruptive. Formal induction sets the standard the $450,000 fleet deserves, and with 6.7% wage inflation a well-trained driver is cheaper than repeated mistakes. A consistent standard also protects the 58% who value flexible booking.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to STT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in STT's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering standards, cost and service quality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how STT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($320 − $200) = $600,000 ÷ $120 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 tour packages a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $320 − $200 = $120. Answer: contribution per unit is $120.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways STT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. STT can compare the 5,000-package break-even with 30,000 packages sold, a margin of safety of 25,000, to see how far bookings can fall before losses begin while the 4.6% cancellation rate persists.
2. The $120 contribution lets partners test a discount: a $10 cut would leave $110, raising break-even to $600,000 ÷ $110 = 5,455 packages, showing how much extra volume a promotion must deliver.
3. Managers can use break-even to check the volume needed to cover $600,000 fixed costs and the hire-purchase instalments on the $450,000 coaches before adding more vehicles.
4. Average total cost of $600,000 ÷ 30,000 + $200 = $220 per package can be compared with the $320 price each quarter to reveal the 11.3% diesel-cost rise and guide the $380 driver training spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 packages | (ii) Contribution per unit = $120 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 30,000 packages; $10 discount and break-even of 5,455; cover for fixed costs and hire purchase; and average total cost of $220 to track 11.3% diesel inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate STT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has STT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.57 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.76 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.17 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.24 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $235,000; 2025 current assets = $75,000 + $110,000 + $70,000 = $255,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $235,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.57; 2025 = $255,000 ÷ $145,000 = 1.76. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($235,000 − $60,000) ÷ $150,000 = $175,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.17; 2025 = ($255,000 − $75,000) ÷ $145,000 = $180,000 ÷ $145,000 = 1.24.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. Cash rose from $45,000 to $70,000 and current liabilities fell from $150,000 to $145,000, so the partnership can meet short-term commitments more comfortably while it pays hire-purchase instalments on the new coaches. The stricter test also improved from 1.17 to 1.24, so STT is not relying on selling inventory to pay debts, and receivables falling from $130,000 to $110,000 means less cash is tied up in unpaid client invoices. Inventories did rise from $60,000 to $75,000, which should be watched, and the ratios are still modest for a travel firm facing 4.6% cancellations.

Conclusion: STT's financial position has improved. Both ratios rose, and the increase does not depend on stock, so the business is better placed to fund the $450,000 coach fleet. The main caution is rising inventories and a small liability base, so the partners should monitor stock before taking on more debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on STT's financial position.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for STT of offering flexible booking on its coach holidays.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey found 58% of 400 clients value flexible booking, so offering it can win bookings from those clients and support the 72% who prefer newer coaches, helping fill the $450,000 fleet at the $320 price; the 7,200 tours sold last quarter show a base to build on. Flexibility also reduces the damage of the 4.6% cancellation rate because guests can move dates instead of demanding refunds.

Disadvantage: Flexible bookings make demand harder to forecast, so STT may struggle to cover $600,000 fixed costs if late changes leave seats empty. Administration rises, adding to the 6 days needed to issue documents and the 34 monthly complaints, while diesel costs up 11.3% must still be paid on every tour whether or not the seat is resold, and with only 3.8% spending growth STT cannot easily raise prices. Flexible terms also complicate scheduling against the 4.6% cancellation rate. Higher standards also help justify the newer coaches to the 58% of clients who value flexible booking.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to STT's survey, cancellations and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.7% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in diesel and coach-maintenance costs will affect STT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): Hire-purchase payments on the $450,000 coaches are usually fixed, so this may not change them directly; if any bank borrowing is variable-rate, a 0.75 percentage point rise would add 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year as an illustrative bound. Higher rates could dampen the 3.8% growth in domestic holidays, but the impact on STT is limited and can be reduced by fixing rates.

Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.23 per hour): With a workforce of 40, drivers' and office pay rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or individual salaries, so a total wage bill cannot be invented; the honest comparison is productivity — 30,000 packages ÷ 40 staff = 750 packages per employee. If the newer coaches keep cancellations at or below 4.6%, the $120 contribution per package can absorb the rise; otherwise margins narrow.

Diesel and maintenance costs (+11.3%): These feed the $200 variable cost per package. As a labelled upper bound, if the whole $200 rose 11.3% that is $22.60 per package (11.3% × $200), or $678,000 a year at 30,000 packages — larger than the $600,000 fixed costs. Even a partial increase cuts the $120 contribution sharply, and the $320 price cannot easily be raised when only 3.8% spending growth is forecast.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in diesel and maintenance costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every package, is far larger than the capped interest effect and the productivity-dependent wage effect, and directly threatens the contribution needed to fund the $450,000 fleet.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to STT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on STT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in STT's context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
